6881: The appellant purchased the land in dispute from the respondent under a sale deed dated March 31, 1959. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to claim the right of pre emption under clause 'fourthly ' of section 15(l)(b). On appeal the District Judge held that the suit was maintainable as the appellant had failed to prove that he was a co sharer in the land. The High Court dismissed the second appeal filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the suit land was owned by more than one person, the right of the co sharer was not available to him. The right of a cosharer is a creamy layer of the statute. [126 D E] (iv) The right which is sought to be enforced against the co sharee is a cretial right of the other co sharers and not a cremental right. [127 A B] (v) The right can be enforced only against the co share holder and not against the co co sharer. [128 D] (vi) The right conferred upon the co sharere d is not a right of preempti ce. 1789: The respondent company was incorporated in January, 1946 as a private limited company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the appellant. Before the Tribunal the Company claimed that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the age of 55 and that the Company should be allowed to continue beyond that age even after the age of 60. The Tribunal held that the Company was not agreeable to adopt the age of retirement at 60 but it allowed the workmen to continue upto 58 years subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 58. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Company 's case was one of an exceptional nature and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the award. HELD: (i) It is well settled that where there are conflicting decisions of the tribunals or courts, the decision of the tribunals may be open to review provided they are satisfied that they are justified in applying the same rules of natural justice. [429 B] (ii)The Company 's contention that it was not correct to say that in recent years at least the tendency in comparable concerns in Bombay region has been to fix the retirement age at 60 cannot be accepted. The Company 's conduct in the past was such that it could not have been expected to change its policy. [430 C D] (iii)It is true that the Company has been making good profits from time to time. But it is equally true that the company has been making profits from time-to-time. It is also true that the practice followed in the past is to reduce the burden of paying the workmen in the past. But it does not follow that the practice of reducing the burden of payment of wages to the workmen must always be regarded as unreasonable. [431 F H] In the present case, the Company 'was not justified in taking the view that it was bound to accept the age of superannuation at 60. [432 A]

3168: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1956 and its shareholders were its directors. 2207: The respondent was a dealer in the business of a dealer. He purchased a business from the appellant and sold it to another. 2593: The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the State of Bombay on October 1, 1948. He declared order dated February 2/4 1955, illegal and void. [922 E] (ii) The Inspector General of Prisons had the report before him and the tentative conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry Officer were bound to influence him, and in depriving the plaintiff of a copy of that report he was handicapped is not knowing what material was influencing the Inspector General. 5538: The appellant was a licensee of the respondent. The respondent had been described as 'licensee ' and the licensor had entered into an agreement with him for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years. The appellant continued in possession by virtue of that agreement. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for eviction on the ground that he was a tenant and also incidentally the appellant was a sub tenant of the respondent and that the appellant had been described to be the licensee. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate court reversed it. In appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was not a licensee and that the respondent was a licensee. In this appeal, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the appellant being a licensee was entitled to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The appellant was not the licensee of the licensee. He was merely a licensee. [811 G] (2) The appellant had granted a licence in respect of certain shop premises to the respondent. It is true that the licence was granted to the respondent under a leave and licence agreement which expired on 31st March, 1966. But the appellant did not take any step to get the licence renewed. The appellant was only a licensee. The respondent was not a sub tenant. The appellant had no right to continue in the premises. [812 D E] (3) The appellant could not claim to have a licence from the licenser. The licence was granted by the licensary to the respondent and the licendor had agreed to allow the licensee to use the premises for the purpose for which the licence was given. The licence had expired on 31 st March, 1966 and the application for eviction was made on or about 1st September, 1965. The appellant could therefore, not be said to be a licensee. Therefore, the appellant was entitled to remain in possession until a decree of ejectment was passed in the suit. [813 F H; 814 A B] (4) The appellant having failed to prove that he was not a tenant, the respondent was entitled to the protection of section 12(1)(b) of the Bombay Rents
4807: The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1973 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, which is respondent in this appeal. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. 1181: The appellants were allotted land in the State of Punjab. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General under section 19(1) of the Act against the order cancelling their quasi permanent allotment in the village Raikot. The Custodian rejected the said revision on the ground that no land was available in the village. The appellants preferred an appeal to the Custodian General which was dismissed by the Additional Custodian on August 20, 1952. Thereafter the appellants moved the Custodian General for restoration of the land to them. The Custodian General made an order on October 31, 1952 cancelling the allotment of the land in the village Raipur and the appellants preferred an application for review of the order cancelling the allotment. The appellants also preferred an application under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of cancellation of the allotment. During the pendency of the revision application the appellants filed an application for a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order cancelling allotment of the quasi permanent allotment. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the power of the Custodian to cancel the quasi permanent allotments was not in conflict with any other provision of the Act or the rules framed thereunder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the power to cancel quasi permanent allotments is conferred by section 19 of the Act on the managing officer or managing corporation constituted under that Act and that the power could be exercised only after the allotment has been cancelled. HELD: (i) The power to cancel a quasi permanent allotment is conferred by the statute itself upon the managing officer and managing corporation constituted or constituted under that statute. The power to do so is conferred by statute itself upon that authority. The power of cancellation of quasi permanent allotments can be exercised either by the managing officer himself or by someone else. If the managing officer has power to cancel the allotment he cannot exercise that power without his consent. [336 B] (ii) The power of the Government to cancel quasipermanent allotment is conferred on the managing office or managing corporation. The power is conferred by Statute on the managing director or managing corporation who are appointed by the Government. The power conferred by Statute is delegated to the managing director. The managing director may delegate that power to another person. But the power to make an order cancelling quasi permanent allotment does not confer on him any power to cancel it

784: The appellant was the owner of certain lands in Madras. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the lease granted to him had been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation, and that he had no right to continue in possession after the date of the grant. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the lease had been granted for a period exceeding one year and that it could not be terminated without compensation under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Act does not provide for any enquiry before the date of vesting of the land in the Government. 2727: The appellant was the hereditary trustee of a temple. He died in 1905 and his successor in office appointed him as trustee. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that he was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Madras Act I of 1925, and for a direction to the respondents to appoint him as trustee of the temple. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not a hereditary trustee but was merely an office holder. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the definition of the trustee is identical in both the Acts; (ii) the appellant being a hereditary trustee was entitled to succeed to the office of trusteeship devolving by hereditary right or was regulated by usage; and (iii) the appellant was a hereditary person within the meaning Of section 6(1)(a). HELD: (i) The appellant was a member of the family of the founder of the temple and was entitled to be appointed as trustee of that temple. [801 G] (ii) The appellant had no right to continue as a trustee of the deity. His appointment was purely temporary and could not be terminated at any time without notice. The term 'hereditary trustee ' has been defined in section 2(11) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, which reads thus: "In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context, "the expression "hereditary" means the person who is in actual possession of the property of the temple, and includes the manager or other trustee in charge of such property." [802 B C] (iv) The appellant being a member of a family governed by the Hindu law, was entitled to hold the office of trustee of the family temple. [882 D E]

The respondents contended that the assessments could not be made on Amarchand and that section 24B had no application to the income received after the death of his father. Held, that the assessments should be made on the respondents as they were entitled to the amount of income tax which accrued to them during the relevant assessment years. The words "in respect of any income" in section 24B are wide enough to include a case where the income is received by a person who has died before the date of the commencement of the Act. The word 'income' in section 24 B means the income received or deemed to have been received by a member of a Hindu undivided Family after the date on which the Act came into force.

[881D E] 2.2 The High Court has struck down the provisions of sec.28 of the Act in the manner of doing away with the restriction imposed by the Administrator on the right of the licensee to carry on business in the licensed premises of the dealer. The High Courts decision is based on the reasoning adopted in Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, II Division, while declaring sec.27(6) in the manner itself is inapplicable. 2065: The appellants were the trustees of a Pachai Kandai Udayavar Temple at Eragudi, in which the respondents were the trustees. They executed a deed of gift in favour of the respondents on May 12, 1929, and obtained a certificate from the Collector under section 88 C.P.C., certifying that the properties had been granted to the respondents as an absolute grant for the performance of certain services in a Matam. The respondents filed an application before the Magistrate for possession of the properties covered by the said deed. The Magistrate held that the respondents had proved their title to the properties in suit and a permanent injunction restraining the respondents from interfering with their possession of the same. The appellants challenged this order in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the respondents ' title in respect of the properties in dispute was open to challenge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the respondents had not established that they had acquired title to the property in question; (ii) the transfer made by the manager not as manager but as an individual was not hit by article 134 B; (iii) the transfer was void ab initio; (iv) the transfer being void ab initia, the possession of the transferee was adverse from the date of the transfer; and (v) the transfer having been made by the Manager not as manager, but as an independent person, the respondents could not claim any right to the properties covered under the deed. HELD: (i) Article 134 B is applicable only where the transfer is made by the managers not as manager or as an individual but as an individuals. [875 F] (ii) The present case falls within the scope of article 134 B. The respondents have failed to establish that they had become owners of the properties mentioned in the deed of gift. [876 G H] (iii) The respondents had not produced any evidence to show that the properties in question belonged to the religious endowment. [877 A] (iv) The respondents have not established that the properties were alienated by the manager of the temple. [878 D]
4641: The appellant, a partnership firm, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cinematograph films. In July, 1966, the appellant applied to the District Magistrate, Jammu for permission to construct a modern cinema hall at the Apsara Theatre in the said building. On July 22, 1969, the District Magistrate granted permission under section 3 of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 to the appellant to erect a modern cinema house. On July 29, 1969, a licence was issued by the District Magistrate to the appellant under section 3(1) of the Act for exhibition of cinematograph films at the Apollo Cinema. On July 30, 1969, an application was made by the appellant for a declaration that the licence was the property of the firm and for inclusion of his name and that of Todar Mal in the said licence as joint licensees. The District Magistrate rejected the application on the ground that the appellant had not produced any evidence to show that he had been authorised by the proprietor or partner of the firm to do so. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the District Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant could not be permitted to raise the question of the validity of the licence. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The High court has rightly held that the appellant was entitled to the grant of a licence under section 3 (1) of The Cinematograph Act. [589E] 2. The High Commissioner 's order is set aside. The District magistrate shall proceed to consider the application afresh after giving the parties a reasonable opportunity of being heard. [590B]
380: The appellants were displaced persons, and the respondent issued a notice to them under section 12 of the , on 30 8 1952, stating that they had committed breaches of certain terms on which the properties had been leased to them. The appellants replied that they had no intention to commit breaches of the terms on which they had been granted leases and that they should be evicted. The appellants filed an application for cancellation of the lease, but the Custodian did not pass any order in respect thereof. On the other hand, the respondent issued notices to the appellants, alleging that they had breached the terms on the various terms on which their properties had been let out to them, and calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled. The appellants contended that section 12 applied only to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself, and that the direction given by the Custodian was beyond his jurisdiction as it applied only to properties of the evacuee and could not affect the rights of the parties in the present appeal. Held, that the appellants were entitled to the relief claimed by them. The power conferred by section 12 is not limited to leases granted under the Act or the rules framed thereunder. It is well settled that the power conferred by the section extends to leases granted for a specified period, and does not extend to leases granted in pursuance of a general power conferred by law. The power to cancel a lease granted under the provisions of the Act is not confined to leases granted before the commencement of the Act. The power of cancelling a lease granted by the Custodian is not limited by the Act to leases granted after the commencement of that Act. The powers of the Custodian are not limited to the grant of leases under the Act.
7109: The appellant was the owner of a land in the State of Rajasthan. He filed an application for exemption from payment of land revenue under section 22 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1956. The Sub Divisional Officer held that Surendrapal Singh, (appellant) aged about 70 years, was a minor son of Raghubir Singh and used to 725 study in Punjab and further held that the land in possession of Raghubirs Singh was ancestral. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Sub Judge was right in his conclusion that Surendra prakash was a minor. His father was a student of the University and was studying in the University. He was a student in the University and had studied in the University
1762: The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of the former State into the Matsya Union. The respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni with which the appeal No. 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former State on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. The appellant contended that the respondent had no right to the goods in question as against the new State of Pepsu and that the respondent was not entitled to the amount due under the contract. Held, that the respondent 's claim based upon the covenant in the Covenant was not enforceable in a court of law. The covenant in the present case did not create any rights in favour of the respondent. The covenant was an act of State and not an act of the State. The covenant did not create a right in favour of a citizen to get his goods exported through the customs department. The covenant merely provided for the recognition of the new sovereign of the existing rights of the residents of the erstwhile State. The respondent was not bound to refund the amount due to him under the contract but it was open to the appellant to recover the amount if it was found that the respondent committed breach of the covenant.
652: The appellants and others were carrying on the business of purchasing and selling cotton, groundnut and groundnut in their respective areas. On January 9, 1953, the Market Committee at Virudhunagar issued a notice stating that the Act and the Rules had come into force in Ramanathapuram District on January 1, 1953, and requiring persons who did business in cotton and groundnuts to take out licences as provided therein. The appellants filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the provisions of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act (Mad XX of 1933) and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the provisions of section 4 A of the Act and rules made thereunder constituted an unreasonable restriction upon the appellants fundamental right to carry on trade or business guaranteed by article 19(1)(g). In appeal to this Court, HELD : The provisions of the Act, and the Rules made thereunder constitute an unreasonable restriction on the appellants ' fundamental right to do business and therefore they are violative of article 19(i)(f) of the Constitution. [439 B] The Act and the rules framed thereunder provide for the regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops in notified area and it is not necessary to examine whether the restrictions imposed are reasonable. [440 C] The Act does not impose any restrictions on the traders in the notified area but imposes certain restrictions on them. It is only when the market committee has been established that the restrictions can be imposed. The Act does no more than impose restrictions on the purchase and sale of agricultural produce in notified area. The Act provides for the establishment of a market committee for every notified area and makes provision for the registration of traders and for the grant of licences for the purchase and sales of such agricultural produce. Section 4A of the Act provides for a scheme of management of the market committee. Under section 4B the State Government may establish a market committee with effect from such date as may be fixed by the State Government. Section 4C provides for the constitution of a market Committee for every notified market area and the same is also provided in section 4D. Section 4E provides for the appointment of a Secretary to the market committee and his duties. Section 4F provides for the delegation of powers of the committee to the Chairman and the
496: The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. They appealed to the High Court against their convictions and sentence. The High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences on the three appellants, Pandurang, Tukaram, Nilia and Bhilia. The High court also confirmed the conviction of the other two accused on the ground that they had been acquitted by the Sessions Judge. The appellants came up in appeal to this Court by special leave. It was contended for them that the convictions should be maintained and that the sentence should be commuted to imprisonment for life. HELD: (i) The convictions must be set aside. The convictions should have been confirmed but not so as to enable the appellants to get a further opportunity to defend themselves. [1085 D] (ii) The High Court has erred in law in confirming the convictions on the ground of non application of mind. The High 'Court has not considered the evidence properly. The High,Court has not given any reasons for its conclusion. [1086 C] (iii) The High court has failed to consider the fact that the deceased was a man of bad character and he could not have been in a position to speak. There is nothing to show that the deceased had any enmity with the appellants or his family members. [1087 E] (iv) The High ' Court has not taken into consideration the fact that there was no eye witness to the occurrence. The prosecution case was that the deceased and his father were attacked by the appellants and others. The deceased was injured and he died at the spot. The appellants were not present at the time when the attack took place. The appellants did not know who the assailants were. Therefore, the possibility of the appellants being falsely implicated cannot be ruled out. [1088 F H] (v) The High, Court has not given reasons why it arrived at the conclusion that the appellants were guilty. [1089 A B]
5397: The petitioner was promoted as Assistant Engineer in Class I service and on 4.9.1965 he was reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer in officiating capacity. On 3.7.1961, he was compulsorily retired from service under Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules as also the power to compulsorily retire a public servant by giving him notice of not less than three months in writing or three months pay and allowances in lieu of such notice. The petitioner challenged the validity of the impugned order on the ground that it violated his fundamental right guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The rule is not violative of Article 14 of The Constitution. [866A] 2.1 The power conferred on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire an employee is absolute and unfettered. It is well settled that the appropriate authority has the absolute right to compulsorily retire any government servant if it is satisfied with respect to his work and conduct either in its inquiry or in the report submitted to it. If there are allegations against the officer concerned and the disciplinary authority comes to the conclusion that the charges are true, he can be compulsorily retired from services. In the instant case, the Government had taken into consideration all relevant materials before making the order of compulsory retirement. Therefore, the order of premature retirement passed by the State Government was clearly without jurisdiction and was liable to be quashed. [867B C] 2.2 The power to compulsorily retiree is vested in the appropriate authority and the same cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [868C] 3.1 The rule does not say that the Government servant who is in Class I or Class II service or post will lose the benefit of the pension. The rule merely says that the Government may at any time reduce the amount of pension. This rule does not apply to the Government servants who have been appointed substantively to a permanent post in class I or class II service or posts. [869D]
4782: The deceased had issued two cheques for Rs. 300 and Rs. 220 respectively in favour of the appellant Corporation on 28th January, 1961. The respondent No. 1 was the agent of the Corporation and the appellant was its agent. On 10th January, 1964, the deceased wrote a letter to the appellant stating that the amount due under the policy was payable by the appellant to the Corporation. The deceased also stated that he would pay the premium in full if the policy was accepted. The deceased replied to the appellant that the premium should be paid in full within one month from the date of receipt of the letter. The deceased however did not accept the proposal and insisted upon the payment of the first premium. The deceased therefore filed a suit against the appellant Corporation for recovery of the amount due and payable under the policy. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the deceased was never informed about the acceptance of the premium; (ii) the two cheques were encashed by the appellant Corporation as they were kept in deposit and credited towards premium account of the proposal; (iii) the two cheque were not encashed and credited towards the premium account of respondent No. 2; (iv) the two receipts were not encashing and credited towards insurance account of the Corporation; and (v) the two amounts were not adjusted towards the premium since the proposal was not considered. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The two cheques were not encahsed and credited towards first premium. [354C] 2.1 There is no evidence to show that the deceased had ever been informed about the receipt of the premium. The fact that the premiums were not encased does not mean that the premium was not paid. It is only when the premiums are encashed that the liability of the Corporation arises. [355D E] 2.2 The two cheques which were encashable were not encashment and were not encadred. The two bills were not encasted. The two receipts were encashes. The two amounts were encashe
2657: The appellant was the owner of a house in which he had been residing. He filed an application for interim injunction restraining the respondent from interfering with his possession and enjoyment of the house. The High Court granted him interim injunction. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the order granting interim injunction was final and could not be challenged under article 133(1) of the Constitution. The expression "final order" in section 205 (1) of Government of India Act, 1935, means an order which finally disposes of the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; if the rights of parties in dispute are determined, it is final as regards the points in dispute in the suit or proceeding. The expression 'final order' in section 205(1) does not mean an order which has finally disposed of the rights in dispute in suit or proceeding but only means an order affecting the decision of the rights. The expression is used in the widest sense to include orders which finally dispose of the rights and obligations of the parties. The expression does not merely connote orders which may be final and conclusive between the parties. It implies an order which is final and conclusive inter se between them. In the case of interlocutory orders, the order is final and cannot be challenged under Article 226.
4451: The appellant, a Hindu, purchased the properties of a Math in 1921 from the personal and separate funds of his predecessor. He was also a trustee for the Math. The Math had two wives, one of whom was a Hindu and the other a Hindu. The Math was a religious institution and the income from the property was received by the Math as its income. The Math claimed that the income was heritable and not joint family property. The Trial Court held that the Math was entitled to the benefit of section 6(1) (a) of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that it could not be said that the Math had acquired any personal or individual property. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The Math was not a Hindu but a Hindu. [663 C] The Math was an institution of which the Math was a manager. The Math being a religious institution, the income derived therefrom must be held to have been applied to the personal or individual use of the Math. [664 D] The Math is a religious institution. It has no personal or individual right to enter into any contract with the Math. It is a religious trust created for the purpose of carrying out the objects of the Math and the income derived from it is not liable to attachment or sale in execution of a decree passed against the Math. Section 6(1)(a) does not apply to a Math. [660 E F] The Math being an institution of a religious nature, the income from its property must be held not to be his personal income. [665 G H; 661 A B]
3292: The appellant, who was the Mahant of a Dera at Patiala, filed a suit for declaration that he was the lawfully appointed mahant of the Dera at Landeke and that he was entitled to manage the properties attached to it. The trial court held that the appellant had no knowledge about the death of Som Dass as to who would become the mahant by election and dismissed the suit. The High Court reversed the decree on appeal. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant did not know about the death and that he could not be said to have knowledge about the date of the death of the deceased. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant was not aware of the death at the time when he died. He was not in possession of the properties of the Dada at Lande. [712B] 2. The appellant had no right to manage the property of the Dasa at Lande or to appoint any person as his mukhtar. The fact that he was not aware about the death does not make him an objector. [713C] 3. The appellant did not take steps to bring on record his legal representatives within the period prescribed. The High court rightly held that the appeal abated. [714D]
4917: The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board (APSEB) and were working in different capacities. They were given a special pay of Rs. 70 per month for the work done by them, but they continued to draw their salary till the age of 58 years. In 1979, the Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification under section 3(1)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Conditions of Service) Act, 1977, fixing the age of retirement from 58 to 55 years. The petitioners challenged the said notification on the ground that it was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that the Government was estopped from reducing the age of superannuation from 58 to 58; and that the decision of the Government was bad for non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of fixation of the age of Retirement. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The decision of the State Government to reduce the age of retirernent is arbitrary and irrational. [550C] 2. The Government has acted arbitrarily in not giving an opportunity to the employees who are similarly situated to meet the case of reduction in the age of superannuating. It is not necessary that the employees should be given an opportunity before reducing the age to retire at the fag end of service. [552E] 3. The Government had taken into consideration all relevant factors including the fact that the employees had been granted a special pay for the work performed by them. The Government did not consider the relevant facts or circumstances bearing upon the question of the age. [553F] 4. The Government could not take into account irrelevant considerations while determining the age of the employees. [554G] 5. The Government cannot fix the age of a person who is already in Government service. The Government can always fix the age with reference to the date of birth of the employee. [556A] 6. The Government is entitled to take into consideration the relevant facts, circumstances and the circumstances of each individual case
6622: The appellant, a manufacturer of milk and milk products, purchased milk from outside the State. The appellant was assessed to sales tax under the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973. The appellant challenged the assessment on the ground that the levy of tax was illegal as it was not in accordance with the provisions of section 9(3) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the levy was invalid as it was contrary to the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 2(p), 6, 7, 8 and 9 of the Act are mandatory and they have to be strictly complied with. [352B] 2.1 The provisions of sections 9 and 10 of the Act have to be read together. They are mandatory in nature. The provisions have to be complied with before any action can be taken or done by the State Government or by any officer of the State Government. [354C] 3.2 The provisions of the Haryana General Sale Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1990 have to be treated as directory. [355E] 3.3 The provisions of Section 9(3)(a) and (b) of the Haryana Act have to he read harmoniously and so construed. [356F] 4.1 The provision of section 9 has to be read along with the provisions contained in section 5 of the Act which provides for the levy of sales tax. [357G]
6521: The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he was in arrears of rent and that the respondent landlord had failed to pay the rent. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate court dismissed the appeal. In second appeal, the High Court held that the order of the Rent Controller fixing fair rent was not final as it was only an interim measure and that the tenant could not be evicted without giving him notice under section 111(h) of the Act. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant landlord that the order passed by the Rent Controller was not final and that the High Court should have remanded the case to the Rent Controller for deciding the question whether the tenant was a tenant in or landlord of the building. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court is set aside and the matter remitted to the Rent Control Tribunal for decision on the question whether there was a valid determination of the fair rent of the premises in dispute. [550C] 2. The Rent Controller has jurisdiction to decide whether the tenant is a tenant in, or landlord of, the building and if so, what the fair rent would be. [551E] 3. The Rent Control Appellate Authority has jurisdiction to determine whether the tenant has been in arrears of the rent for more than six months and whether the tenant had committed defaults in payment of rent within one month from the date of service of summons. The Rent controller has jurisdiction to pass an order of eviction. [552A B] 4. The Rent Controllers are empowered to fix fair rent of any building in which the landlord resides or carries on business or personally works for gain. [553B] 5. The Rent Controlling Authority has jurisdiction only to determine whether there is a valid determination. [554D] 6. The Rent Review Committee has power to review its own orders. [556F]
3602: The respondent was a member of the State Forest Service. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Conservator of Forests in the year 1966, and was confirmed as such on December 1, 1966. In the provisional list of officers prepared under section 115 of the , he was shown at serial No. 2 while the petitioner was shown at Serial No. 3. The petitioner challenged the seniority list before the High Court by filing a writ petition which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had erred in holding that the list was provisional and not final; that the High court should have directed the preparation of a fresh list after hearing objections. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962 is ultra vires and illegal. [830G] (2) The High court was wrong in holding that a list prepared under section 116 of the Act was provisional. It was not open to the High Court to direct the preparation of another list after hearing objection. [831A] (3) The High 'Court could not issue a writ of certiorari for quashing the seniority list. [832B]
6647: The petitioners in the writ petitions filed by them were granted Export House Certificates for import of certain items to export houses. They had also applied for import of the said items under the Import Policy 1978 1979. The Import Policy 1978, 1979 and 1980 made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said Policy. In para 174 of the said policy it was provided that the Additional licences issued to Export Houses will also be valid for the import of the following items upto 10% (upto 15% in the case of Trading Houses) of the value of the licence for: (i) Import of technical designs, drawings and other technical documentation for a value not exceeding Rs. 10 lakhs in the case the export houses; (ii) import of items appearing in Appendices 1 Part A, 3 Part B and 5 Part C subject to the following conditions: "(a) that the c.i.f. value of a `single item ' on the basis of 10% as at (a) above, works out to less than Rupees one lakh, import would be permitted upto a value of Rs. 1 lakh, provided it is within the overall flexibility allowed on the licence; (b) where the value for import of a `different item ' on account of diversification of exports is more than Rs. 10 lakh, import will be permitted upto Rs. 1 crore, provided it has been established beyond doubt that the exporters have been able to produce sufficient evidence to show that they are entitled to the benefit of the import facilities. " The petitioners who had been granted Export House Certificate for import of various items in terms of the Import Policy, 1978 1979 and 1980 respectively filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid two notifications. The petitioners contended that there was no similarity between the petitioners who had obtained the Export House Certificates and the petitioners who were granted Additional Licences on the basis that they had been granted Additional Licenses. It was further submitted that the petitioners had been discriminated against inasmuch as they had been denied the benefit of an additional licence on the ground that they had not produced sufficient evidence to prove their claim that they had actually exported the goods. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court
5471: The appellant was a director of a company. He had been in possession of the flat in question for more than six years and he had been in occupation thereof for over two decades. In the complaint filed by him under section 630 of the Act, the appellant alleged that he had obtained possession of the said flat from the company on behalf of the company without any authority or consent and that he had not taken any steps to obtain the same. The company was served with a notice of eviction under section 628 of the Act. The appellant contended that the provisions contained in section 630 were not applicable to the facts of the case as the company was not in possession of any residential accommodation at all and that the company was entitled to evict the appellant under section 629(1) of the Act and that the provisions of section 630 did not apply to the facts and circumstances of the case. Held: (i) Section 630 does not apply to cases where the company is in possession of a residential accommodation for over three years before the institution of the prosecution against an officer or employee of the company. (ii)The word "officer" occurring in sub section (1) of section 629 must be construed as including the present officers and employees of a company but not of the company and the expression "any such property" in section 629 cannot include the property of a company which has been in possession for over three decades. (iii)The word 'officer ' in section 628 means not only the officer who is in actual possession of the premises but also the person in charge of the premises. (iv)The word `officer ' in sub section 1 of section 628 includes both the officer in actual possession and the person in control of the premises and the person incharge of the premises can be said to be in actual possession.
3442: The appellant, a Hindu, was the owner of a property called "Shishya" and the Sansthan was constituted under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The Sansthan was established in 1948 for the purpose of providing religious worship to the public at large. The appellant 's predecessor in interest had been managing the affairs of the Sansthan. After the passing of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950, an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons Bhaskarrao Chimanrao Deshmukh, Ramrao Sahebrao Deshpande, Ramrao Shakamdas Deshpan vs Sayaji Kulkarni, and Ramrao Sahabrao Deshmaneshwar vs Sayajirao Krishnarao Deshpane, and the Charity Commissioner by his order dated August 25, 1956, held the Sansthan to be a public trust and ordered its registration as a public trust under the Act. The appellant challenged the order of the Charity Commissioner before the High Court on the ground that the Sansthan being a private institution was not a public trust within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act and that the Sanad issued by the Government did not confer any title on the appellant. Held, that the Sanathan was a public charitable trust and the Sanad merely provided for the maintenance of the Sanctrine and the Sanctor were not entitled to interfere with the management of the Sanctor. The Sanath could not be said to have been appointed by the Government to manage the affairs of a public trust. The Sanhant was not a trustee but was merely a manager. The Sananta was not a manager of a public religious endowment. The Sanant was not a holder of a public office and the Sananta was merely a person who could
362: The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 1952. He did not pay up the assessed amount of tax but only issued a recovery certificate under section 46(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer on the 10th April 1951 issued a notice of demand against him for payment of the assessed amount. The assessee 's contention that section 46(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act is void under article 13(1) of the Constitution was rejected by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. On appeal the Appellate Tribunal held that the Income tax Officer had no power to issue a recovery certificate in respect of the balance of the tax due from the assessee. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that section 46 (2) of Act 46 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, which authorises the Collector to issue a warrant of arrest and detention in satisfaction of the demand, is ultra vires article 14 of the Constitution as the same offends article 22(1) and (2), article 21 and article 14 of Constitution. Held, that section 46 of the Income Tax Act, 1922 is valid under article 13 of the Constitution. Section 46(2), which authorises the Collectors in different States to adopt machinery for the recovery of income tax, does not confer any additional powers on the Collector to recover the arrears of tax. The words "any other law" in section 46(3) are wide enough to include all such laws which have been passed before the Constitution. The HighCourt also suggested that in case of difference of opinion between two members of the Committee, the matter should be referred to a third member. [294D] (3) The High Cou rt had no power to give directions to the Government to make any other recommendation or to create any post.
